title: How the most successful B2B startups found their original idea: past pain, ponder and probe, present pull
summary: Lenny synthesizes interviews with two dozen B2B founders (Gong, Notion, Figma, Retool, Slack, etc.) into a framework for finding a startup idea. A great idea is important, underserved, and something you're excited about. Founders found it through three paths, always chasing "pain" and "pull".

principles.text: A great B2B idea is important, underserved, and something you're excited to spend years on.
principles.quote: Find an idea that solves a problem that is important, underserved, and that you’re excited about.

principles.text: Venture-scale needs a big market: most startups fail because the market is too small, not the idea.
principles.quote: Most startups fail not because the idea isn’t good but because the market for the solution is just too small.

principles.text: Your solution must beat the existing one by 4 points out of 10 (Delta-4); a 6+ incumbent is very hard to replace.
principles.quote: Your solution needs to be +4 better for anyone to care about your product.

principles.text: Three reliable paths to an idea: past pain, ponder and probe, present pull.
principles.quote: Across all of the interviews I did, I found three reliable paths for discovering a great idea:

principles.text: Whatever the path, look for both pain (important problem) and pull (you're actually solving it).
principles.quote: Pain tells you there’s an opportunity to solve a problem, and that it’s important. Pull tells you that you’re actually solving the problem.

principles.text: Whiteboarding works only if you pick a space and talk to customers quickly; otherwise ideas stay abstract.
principles.quote: There’s a wrong way of whiteboarding and a right way (i.e. ideating and building in a silo versus quickly talking to potential users to validate your idea).
